how-to-develop-leadership-skills-in-chil:
Leadership at this age is not charisma or being in charge. It is three ordinary capacities that can be built deliberately, and none of them requires a title.

What it actually consists of

Taking responsibility for something that affects others. Not a task, an outcome. The difference between being asked to bring the equipment and being the person the equipment depends on.

Perspective-taking. Noticing what other people need, including the quiet one who has not said anything. This is the capacity that separates a leader from somebody loud.

Speaking up when it is uncomfortable. Saying the unpopular thing, or saying stop. This one is closer to courage than to skill and it is built in small doses.

Where children practise it

Not in leadership programmes. In situations with a real outcome and no adult managing it.

Organising a game with younger children. Being responsible for one part of a family event. Teaching a sibling something. Running a stall. Captaining anything. Looking after a pet the household depends on them for.

The common feature is that something genuinely does not happen if they do not do it.

What to do as an adult

Hand over whole things. Not steps. "You are in charge of the picnic" produces different behaviour from a list of picnic tasks, because it includes the planning and the noticing.

Let it go wrong. A child whose plan fails and who has to deal with the disappointment of others has learned something no successful, adult-rescued project teaches.

Debrief without judging. What worked, what would you do differently, what did the others need that you missed. This is where the reflection happens, and skipping it means the experience teaches less.

Notice the quiet version. The child who makes sure everyone is included, or who calms a dispute, is leading. Naming that is important, because otherwise children conclude leadership means being the loudest.

What does not build it

Titles without responsibility. Being told they are a natural leader, which produces a performance. Competitive exercises where somebody must win. And adult-designed activities where the outcome is guaranteed.

The bit worth saying to a child

That being in charge mostly means being the one who carries it when it goes wrong, and doing the parts nobody else wants. Children who understand that early either want it or do not, and both answers are fine.

The aim is not a child who leads. It is a child capable of it when the situation calls for it, and content when it does not.
decision-making-activities-for-kids:
Deciding well is built through small, real, reversible choices. Not through exercises, and not through being given options that do not matter.

The principle

A decision is only practice if the child lives with the outcome. Choosing between two things you would be equally happy with teaches nothing; choosing between two things where one turns out worse teaches everything.

Which means the useful activities all share one feature: a genuine consequence, small enough that it does not matter much.

Two acceptable options, from three

Red coat or blue coat. Apple or banana. This does not feel like decision-making and it is the foundation: the experience of one thing closing when another opens.

Spend their own money, from five

A small amount, in a shop, with no veto. The disappointing purchase is the lesson. This is the single most effective decision-making activity there is and it costs a few pounds.

Plan a family evening, from seven

Meal, activity, timing. They decide, everybody lives with it, including when it is a bit dull. Debrief afterwards without saying you told them so.

Pick the route, from seven

On a walk or a journey, give them the map. Getting slightly lost is the useful part.

The two-column list, from nine

Write reasons for and against, out loud, together. The value is not the list; it is discovering that reasons can be weighed rather than merely felt.

Choose which thing to drop, from nine

Too many activities, not enough evenings. Let them decide what goes. Trade-offs under real constraint is the hardest and most useful version.

Predict then check, any age

Before deciding, ask what they think will happen. Afterwards, ask whether it did. This builds the feedback loop that turns experience into judgement, and without it a child can make a hundred decisions and learn from none.

Spend a fixed budget on a real thing, from eleven

The birthday, the trip, the week's shopping. Fixed amount, real constraints, their call.

What to do when they choose badly

Nothing, mostly. No rescue, no purchase to replace it, and no observation about what you would have done.

Later, when the sting has gone, ask what they would do differently. That question converts a bad outcome into judgement; a lecture converts it into resentment.

What to avoid

False choices, which children detect immediately. Too many options, which paralyses. Decisions too large for their age, which is frightening rather than empowering. And overturning their decision after giving it to them, which teaches that the handover was not real.

Judgement is not taught. It is accumulated, out of a great many small decisions with real outcomes, starting far earlier than most households allow.
problem-solving-skills-for-children:
Solving a problem has four stages, and children get stuck at different ones. Knowing which one your child stalls at is more useful than general encouragement to keep trying.

Stage one: noticing there is a problem

Sounds trivial and is not. Some children push on with an approach that is visibly failing because they have not registered that it is failing.

Built by: asking is that working, rather than pointing out that it is not. Over time the question becomes internal.

Stage two: working out what the problem actually is

The stage adults skip most often on children's behalf. A child says the tower keeps falling; the actual problem is that the base is too narrow. Getting from the symptom to the cause is most of the work.

Built by: asking why they think it is happening, and waiting. Not supplying the answer, which is very tempting because you can see it.

Stage three: trying something

Where children who are afraid of being wrong get stuck. A child who will not attempt anything until they are sure is not lacking ideas; they are avoiding the visible failure.

Built by: a household where attempts that fail are unremarkable, and where adults visibly try things that do not work.

Stage four: adjusting

The one that separates persistence from repetition. Some children try the same thing eleven times with more force. Trying something different is the skill.

Built by: asking what else could we try, and by explicitly naming the shift when it happens: you changed your approach there.

What to do when they are stuck

Wait longer than is comfortable. Count to twenty. Most children solve it in the silence, and every time an adult fills that silence the child loses a repetition of the entire cycle.

If they are genuinely stuck, ask rather than tell. What have you tried? What happens if you do that bit first? Which part is the hard bit?

That last question is unusually useful, because narrowing a problem to its difficult part is itself the skill.

Where it gets practised

Building things that fall down. Cooking something that goes wrong. Games with a strategy. Fixing a bike. Getting somewhere without directions. Any situation with a real obstacle and no adult removing it.

Screens are poor for this specifically because the feedback is instant and the retry is free, which removes the part where you have to think before acting.

What undermines it

Rescuing, which is the main one. Praising quick answers, which teaches that speed is the measure. Correcting the approach rather than letting the approach fail. And doing the difficult part yourself to keep things moving, which is nearly always the part worth leaving.

A child who has been allowed to be stuck, repeatedly, with somebody nearby but not intervening, is building something no worksheet provides.
entrepreneurship-activities-for-kids:
A real small venture teaches costing, failure and customers faster than any lesson about business. The rule that makes it work is the one adults find hardest: you may not do the difficult parts for them.

What makes it real

Three conditions. Real money, however little. Real customers who are not obliged to buy. And a genuine possibility of losing.

A stall where relatives buy everything out of kindness teaches nothing, and children know it is happening.

Seven to nine: the simplest version

A stall. Lemonade, biscuits, bracelets, plants grown from cuttings. The learning is in the parts adults usually take over: working out what the ingredients cost, deciding a price, and discovering afterwards whether they made or lost money.

Do the arithmetic with them at the end, honestly, including when the answer is that they lost two pounds.

Nine to eleven: a service

Washing cars, walking a neighbour's dog, weeding, packing shopping. Services teach pricing your time, which is a harder and more useful idea than pricing an object.

Also teaches turning up when you do not feel like it, which is most of what running anything consists of.

Eleven to fourteen: making something people actually want

Baked goods to order. Repairing or reselling. Something they design and produce. This is where the interesting failure happens: making twenty of something nobody wanted.

Introduce the idea of asking first. Would you buy this, and at what price, before making any of it.

Fourteen and up: the real thing

Tutoring, a market stall, something online, a small commission. Real customers, real accounts, real complaints. At this age it can genuinely be theirs.

The concepts, in the order they arrive

Cost and price are different, and the gap is the profit. Children routinely price below cost until they have done the sum once.

Somebody has to want it. The commonest lesson, learned by making something nobody buys.

Your time is worth something. Arrives with services.

Reputation compounds. The second dog walk comes from doing the first one properly.

The rules for the adult

Do not fund losses. Do not buy the stock out of pity. Do not take over when it is going badly. Do not tidy their pricing. Answer questions and no more.

A venture rescued by a parent is a lesson in being rescued.

What it is actually for

Not producing a young entrepreneur. It is one of the few available situations where a child experiences the whole loop, deciding, doing, being judged by reality, and adjusting, with stakes small enough to be safe.

The failure is the most valuable part, which is why it must be allowed to happen.
